claims.text: The substrate is uncoated Zircaloy-4 nuclear-fuel cladding in its standard operational form.
A roughly 100 nm alumina coating doped with 3–5 mol% yttria will be deposited on Zircaloy-4 by ALD.
The coated material will undergo preliminary adhesion and interfacial-compatibility testing under cyclic thermal-mechanical loading.
Oxidation performance will be tested in steam at 1200 °C for 2 hours.
The coating will form a dense, continuous ceramic film on Zircaloy-4.
The yttria-doped alumina film will adhere strongly to Zircaloy-4 under cyclic thermal-mechanical loading.
Yttria doping stabilizes protective alpha-Al2O3 at high temperature.
Yttria doping reduces grain-boundary diffusion of oxygen through the alumina coating.
Yttria doping improves thermal-expansion matching and minimizes coating-substrate interfacial stresses.
Maintaining coating adhesion prevents spallation and preserves the oxygen-barrier function.
A preliminary adhesion study ensures that the coating remains intact during cyclic thermal-mechanical stresses.
Relative to uncoated Zircaloy-4, the coated cladding will have a significantly lower high-temperature oxidation rate.
The lower oxidation rate will be evidenced by reduced oxide-scale thickness and reduced mass gain.
The coated cladding will retain mechanical integrity better than uncoated Zircaloy-4 after high-temperature oxidation and cyclic loading.
Improved oxidation resistance is conditional on the coating remaining adherent during service-like cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
Failure of interfacial adhesion during prolonged cycling may limit the coating's effectiveness.
Absence of a statistically significant reduction in both oxide-scale thickness and mass gain relative to an uncoated control will falsify the hypothesis.
Spallation or delamination during the initial cyclic adhesion evaluation will falsify the hypothesis.
